question: After controlling architecture and token parallelism, which generation operations genuinely enlarge the time-space computational power of autoregressive and masked-diffusion Transformers, and can a masked model learn rewrite, insertion, and deletion operations well enough to exploit that power?

key_findings.claim: A standard masked diffusion model can simulate a uniform CREW PRAM in asymptotically optimal parallel time, but its context must retain the computation trace and therefore scales with total work.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 maps a PRAM using P(n) processors for T(n) rounds to a constant-depth, logarithmic-width encoder Transformer MDM with O(P(n)T(n)) context and O(T(n)) decoding steps. Appendix H realizes one PRAM round as eight persistent tokens per processor and appends another round rather than overwriting old state.

anchors.section: Appendix H, Theorem 8 and PRAM trace construction

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's dense-attention, finite-precision, monotone-unmasking model, an MDM with context S(n) has at most soft-O(S(n)^3) serial computation available.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 and its proof count soft-O(S(n)^2) FLOPs per encoder forward pass and use T(n) <= S(n), because at least one fresh token is revealed per step, to obtain soft-O(S(n)^3) total work. The paper interprets this as a barrier to super-polynomial-time reasoning at polynomial context, not as an unconditional lower bound on every diffusion architecture or external-memory system.

key_findings.claim: Any-order generation alone does not enlarge expressivity once architecture and one-token-per-step decoding are controlled in the paper's model.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 constructs a Masked-ARM with O(S(n)) length and a constant number of extra layers that emits each any-order MDM update as an address-token pair in chronological order. The construction shows that attention can reconstruct the MDM state and choose the same next position and content, while leaving parallel token emission as a separate advantage.

key_findings.claim: Any-Process MDM adds learned remask, insert, and delete controls to ordinary unmasking while keeping one encoder backbone and three small binary heads.
key_findings.evidence: Each position receives a three-bit control: remask converts an existing token back to a mask, insert appends a new mask after a position, and delete removes a position that was already masked. Equation 4 fixes their composition order; Appendix C gives four losses and Algorithm 1. The self-supervised losses are presented as possible objectives, whereas all reported task experiments use explicit state-transition supervision generated by known algorithms.

anchors.section: 4.1 An Instantiation with Unmask, Remask, Insert, and Delete
Appendix C.1-C.4, architecture, objectives, and inference

key_findings.claim: Rewrite capability removes the persistent-trace overhead in the formal PRAM simulation, yielding O(S(n)) context and O(T(n)) decoding steps for a PRAM that itself uses S(n) memory and T(n) rounds.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4 first simulates a Rewrite-MDM transition with three AP-MDM phases—insert alternating masks, unmask new positions while remasking old ones, then delete old masks—and then overwrites fixed processor and memory regions. This supports the paper's PSPACE-versus-P statement when context is polynomial and arbitrarily many inference steps are permitted, but it is an existence construction with the PRAM program encoded in Transformer parameters rather than a learned solver guarantee.

key_findings.claim: The Sudoku experiment reports 99.28% accuracy for AP-MDM, but its apparent data-efficiency advantage is not established by a like-for-like sample accounting.
key_findings.evidence: The main comparison uses a 1.2M-parameter AP-MDM trained from 100 hard puzzles versus published ARM and AO-MDM results trained from 1.8M puzzles with 42M and 6M parameters, respectively; the reported accuracies are 99.28%, 87.18%, and 89.49%. Appendix N says each of the 100 puzzles yields 25,022.6 supervised state-transition tuples on average—about 2.5M transition examples—and, in the immediately preceding sentence, inconsistently reports 1,421.3 tuples per puzzle. Thus the unit of supervision differs substantially from the headline puzzle count.

anchors.section: 5.1 Sudoku Puzzles, Figure 3 and comparison table

key_findings.claim: The exact-support separation for two-sided Dyck-k is a sharply qualified formal result rather than evidence about ordinary softmax language generation.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5/12 constructs a stochastic AP-MDM that inserts two distinct mask types and samples with zero-temperature hardmax so that its support is exactly the two-sided Dyck-k language. The ARM impossibility applies to fixed constant-depth, polylog-width Transformers under the assumption TC0 != NC1; finite-temperature softmax, approximate support, scalable depth, or external editing are outside the statement.

key_findings.claim: On the synthetic minimum-cut trace task, AP-MDM preserves almost perfect accuracy as graph size grows while the matched ARM trace generator rapidly fails.
key_findings.evidence: For 4, 5, and 6 nodes, ARM accuracy falls from 90.32% to 43.04% to 0.30%, while AP-MDM reports 100% at all three sizes and 99.99%, 99.97%, 99.92% for 7, 8, and 10 nodes; ARM results above six nodes are not reported. Both use the same 8-layer, 256-hidden architecture and 100K generated graph instances, but AP-MDM receives parallel Edmonds-Karp state transitions while ARM must serialize every operation into much longer sequences.

Appendix O, graph trajectory and ARM encoding

key_findings.claim: The parity result demonstrates strong algorithm-trace extrapolation from four atomic transition examples, but not unqualified generalization to mathematically arbitrary lengths.
key_findings.evidence: The AP-MDM learns to remask zeros or pairs of ones and delete the masks, and the paper reports 100% on 1,000 random variable-length test sequences after training on four length-two transitions with an approximately 200-parameter model. The implementation section simultaneously lists maximum sequence length 3, leaving the exact tested length range and how longer initial sequences bypass that limit under-specified.

anchors.section: Appendix P, Data and ARM Baseline

key_findings.claim: The claimed hardness of serializing arbitrary edit histories rests on an explicit unproved complexity conjecture.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 6/13 reduces an Editing-Query task to PRESERVES, a dynamic-list update problem. The critical step is Conjecture 14 that PRESERVES is DLOGTIME-uniform NC1-hard; without that conjecture, the stated constant-depth ARM separation does not follow. This is materially weaker evidence than the unconditional simulation upper bounds.

method.core_idea: Treat the generation procedure itself as a computational resource model, isolate parallelism and ordering from editability, then extend a masked diffusion model with learned remask, insert, and delete controls so it can revise content and reuse sequence space.
method.mechanism: The theory relates fixed-depth encoder MDM steps to CREW PRAM rounds through an E-FASP programming abstraction, serializes any-order updates into address-token pairs to compare against Masked-ARM, and uses overwritable fixed memory to show an AP-MDM PRAM simulation. The implementation shares one bidirectional Transformer across an unmask vocabulary head and three binary operation heads. In reported experiments, task-specific solvers generate supervised intermediate states and control bits for Sudoku backtracking, Edmonds-Karp graph editing, and parity elimination; inference repeatedly applies all predicted edits until convergence or a task stop token.
assumptions: Encoder and decoder Transformers have fixed depth and heads, logarithmic or polylogarithmic embedding width, finite-precision arithmetic, and the positional encodings and hard-attention primitives required by E-FASP.
Standard MDM decoding is monotone: at least one token is permanently unmasked per step and decoded positions cannot be reused.
The PRAM program and instruction lookup can be hard-coded into Transformer parameters; the expressivity theorems do not require gradient training to discover the program.
The CREW PRAM reference permits concurrent reads but excludes write conflicts, and all addresses, processor identifiers, and words fit in logarithmic width.
A learned edit controller can identify errors, branch points, removable state, and stopping conditions from current sequence context.
Task-specific algorithm traces are available and accurately label every unmask, remask, insertion, and deletion decision for the empirical studies.
The proposed corruption-based self-supervised objectives provide useful proxies for real revision behavior, although that premise is not tested in the paper's experiments.
Exact language-support claims may use zero-temperature hardmax and two mask-token types rather than the ordinary one-mask, finite-temperature MDM setup.
The formal ARM comparison excludes architectures with writable external memory, explicit reduction systems such as PENCIL, growing depth, tools, or non-Transformer controllers.
Theorem 13 additionally assumes the paper's PRESERVES problem is DLOGTIME-uniform NC1-hard.

techniques.role: Separates token parallelism, generation order, rewritability, and dynamic length so each claimed advantage can be attributed to a specific operation.
Expresses constant-depth encoder Transformer computations as full-access sequence programs used in the PRAM simulations.
Measures decoding steps as parallel time and token context as a memory or persistent-work budget.
Shows a one-token-per-step Masked-ARM can encode any-order MDM updates as where-to-write and what-to-write pairs.
Turns selected decoded tokens back into masks so the model can correct mistakes and revisit branches.
Adds blank positions at arbitrary locations, permitting adaptive sequence growth and structure-relative generation.
Reclaims positions after remasking, reducing active context and enabling variable-length output.
Simulates in-place replacement by inserting alternating masks, transferring new values, and deleting the old masked cells.
Converts known solvers into per-step token and operation labels for Sudoku, max-flow/min-cut, and parity.
Proposes distinct corruption objectives for unmasking, error remasking, insertion, and redundant-mask deletion, though these objectives are not empirically evaluated.
Allows generation to stop on EOS, sequence convergence, repeated-state detection, or an iteration cap rather than a fixed all-unmasked endpoint.

evaluations.setting: Uniform CREW PRAM simulation by fixed-depth, log-width encoder MDM and AP-MDM constructions
evaluations.metric: Asymptotic decoding steps and maximum context length
evaluations.result: MDM uses O(T) steps and O(PT) context; AP-MDM uses O(T) steps and O(S) context for a PRAM with P processors and S memory
evaluations.baseline: Autoregressive or masked generation that cannot overwrite persistent computation state

evaluations.baseline: Published ARM at 87.18% with 42M parameters and AO-MDM at 89.49% with 6M parameters, both trained from 1.8M puzzles

evaluations.result: Constructed AP-MDM support equals the language for arbitrary length
evaluations.baseline: Fixed constant-depth, polylog-width ARM under TC0 != NC1

evaluations.baseline: Matched ARM operation-triplet generator falls from 90.32% at four nodes to 0.30% at six nodes and is unreported for larger graphs

evaluations.result: A conditional separation is claimed through the Editing-Query reduction

evaluations.result: Trainability is argued from four explicit losses but not demonstrated

limitations: Author-stated: the particular remask, insert, and delete definitions are sufficient rather than necessary, and other transition designs may offer the same formal advantages.
Author-stated: learning token order is substantially harder than learning which Sudoku values to unmask, as reflected by slower control-head loss convergence.
Author-stated: exact simulation of edit operations by an ARM becomes possible if resource limits are relaxed and sufficiently contrived intermediate summaries are allowed.

Reviewer-identified: every reported AP-MDM task experiment uses privileged trajectories from a known solver; none tests the proposed self-supervised operation losses on natural text, code revisions, proofs, or scientific objects.

Reviewer-identified: the three component operations and iterative editing substantially predate the paper in LevT, PENCIL, ReMDM, FlexMDM, and Edit Flows; the contribution is the particular unification and complexity analysis rather than invention of editing generation.

Reviewer-identified: the headline Sudoku comparison mixes puzzle counts, transition-tuple counts, model sizes, and results imported from another paper. Appendix N both reports 1,421.3 and 25,022.6 transitions per puzzle, an unresolved internal inconsistency.

Reviewer-identified: 100 Sudoku puzzles yielding roughly 2.5M labeled transitions do not establish orders-of-magnitude lower supervision than 1.8M whole-puzzle examples without a token-, transition-, and compute-matched comparison.

Reviewer-identified: all empirical domains are synthetic algorithm imitation; there is no scaled language-model evaluation, no real repository edit history, and no molecular or biological generation despite broad claims about code and science.

Reviewer-identified: no repeated-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals, training FLOPs, inference FLOPs, wall-clock comparisons, or systematic edit-head ablations are reported for the headline results.

Reviewer-identified: Theorem 2 depends on dense self-attention cost, logarithmic width, finite precision, and T <= S monotone decoding; it should not be read as a universal lower bound on diffusion models with sparse attention, reusable latent state, tools, or external memory.

Reviewer-identified: the PSPACE statement is an expressivity inclusion with potentially exponential test-time steps and a hard-coded PRAM program, not evidence that gradient learning finds useful PSPACE algorithms.

Reviewer-identified: Theorem 5 changes the standard setup by using two mask types and hardmax, and its ARM lower bound is conditional on TC0 != NC1 and exact support rather than approximate generation quality.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 6 rests on the unproved NC1-hardness Conjecture 14 for PRESERVES, so the paper's strongest no-ARM-simulation claim is conditional twice over.

Reviewer-identified: the implementation declares maximum parity sequence length 3 while claiming generalization to arbitrary input lengths; the tested length range and actual positional-encoding behavior are not documented clearly enough to reconcile these statements.

Reviewer-identified: the deletion primitive can remove only a position already containing a mask, so deleting an ordinary token requires a coordinated multi-step remask-delete trajectory and can fail or loop if the controller desynchronizes.

Reviewer-identified: binary insertion permits at most one new mask after each current position per step; rapid growth is exponential across steps and can itself cause a context or FLOP explosion without a resource-aware stop policy.
Reviewer-identified: flexible stopping by convergence or repeated state prevents some infinite loops but offers no correctness certificate and may accept a stable, invalid output.

Reviewer-identified: the paper compares against a restricted ARM, not the broader class of autoregressive systems with PENCIL-style reduction, editable scratchpads, program interpreters, or external search.
failure_modes: A remask head mistakes uncertainty for error, repeatedly erasing correct tokens and spending extra inference compute without progress.
A locally plausible edit introduces a global constraint violation that the tokenwise control heads cannot detect.
Remask and unmask oscillate between two sequences until a loop detector halts on an invalid state.
Insertion probabilities remain active and double the active sequence repeatedly, exhausting memory before a useful structure forms.
Deletion fires before useful masked state is restored, losing information needed to recover the branch or object structure.
Parallel edits interfere semantically even when the formal CREW memory-write condition is satisfied.
The training trajectory covers one solver's canonical state order, so a small off-trajectory inference error produces states with no supervised recovery action.
A known algorithm's trace labels leak the solution procedure, making sample efficiency appear to come from the generation paradigm rather than richer supervision.
A finite-temperature approximation assigns nonzero probability outside the exact-support language established only for hardmax.
The fixed-depth Transformer cannot reliably extrapolate address arithmetic, graph encodings, or branch-color conventions beyond training sizes.
A task lacks trustworthy intermediate-process data, causing the proposed self-supervised insert/delete corruption labels to favor surface reconstruction rather than meaningful revision.
A stopping rule based on EOS or state repetition terminates prematurely because the model is confidently wrong.
The theoretically optimal space simulation performs many expensive full-context forward passes, making its wall-clock or energy cost worse than a specialized serial solver.
An ARM with an explicit memory-reduction primitive invalidates the practical relevance of a separation proved only against append-only generation.
reusable_insights: Analyze generation operators separately from backbone architecture: parallel token count, write order, overwrite, insertion, deletion, and stopping are independent design axes.
Treat context length as a memory resource and decoding steps as parallel time, but report total work and wall time alongside both.
Persistent traces are a hidden space tax; allowing revision or garbage collection can matter more than allowing arbitrary token order.
A formal expressivity construction should be paired with a learnability experiment that removes hard-coded programs and privileged trajectories.
Operation heads make edit semantics human-readable and ablatable, which is preferable to an opaque monolithic transition when diagnosing failures.
Train controllers on recovery states produced by the model itself, not only clean expert trajectories, to reduce edit-policy compounding error.
Use a progress invariant or verifier for editable generation so extra test-time compute is measured against correctness rather than mere state changes.
Count supervision in tokens and transitions, not just source objects, when algorithm traces expand one example into thousands of labeled states.
Compare editable models against equally editable autoregressive baselines, including explicit scratchpad compaction and external-memory systems.
Separate exact-support theory from finite-temperature probability mass, calibration, and benchmark quality.
Variable-length generation needs explicit resource controls because the same insertion mechanism that removes a fixed canvas can create runaway context growth.
Synthetic parity, Dyck, Sudoku, and graph tasks are useful unit tests for individual operations, but real edit histories are needed to validate the claimed domain transfer.
A current practical benchmark should include ReMDM, FlexMDM, Edit Flows, PRISM, ProSeCo, and token-editing diffusion under one backbone, data mixture, and compute budget.
open_questions: Can one pretrained AP-MDM learn remask, insert, and delete from ordinary text and code corpora without solver-generated transition labels?
Which training target reliably distinguishes a globally wrong token from a locally uncertain but valid alternative without a verifier?
Does joint editability still help after controlling for the much richer transition supervision given to AP-MDM?
How do accuracy, sequence length, number of edits, total FLOPs, latency, and energy scale jointly as the inference budget increases?
Can the Sudoku tuple-count inconsistency be corrected and the comparison rerun with equal numbers of labeled transitions, tokens, parameters, and training FLOPs?
What exact parity lengths were tested, and can the maximum-sequence-length-3 implementation reproduce extrapolation by orders of magnitude with fixed positional encodings?
Can a softmax, finite-precision AP-MDM approximate the two-sided Dyck support with a quantitatively bounded invalid-mass rate as length grows?
Is PRESERVES actually DLOGTIME-uniform NC1-hard, or can Theorem 6 be replaced by an unconditional separation?
What is the tight computational class of MDMs under sparse or linear attention, growing depth, cached state, and non-monotone schedules?
Can a resource-aware edit policy guarantee termination and monotonic expected progress without eliminating useful backtracking?
How does AP-MDM compare with PENCIL, LevT, Edit Flows, FlexMDM, PRISM, ProSeCo, and LLaDA2.1 on the same real code-edit and reasoning workloads?
Do insert and delete provide gains beyond direct token-to-token substitution when output length is fixed?
Can model-generated failed trajectories, process supervision, reinforcement learning, or verifier feedback replace hand-coded algorithm traces safely?
Which edit operations remain reliable at billion-parameter scale, and do their control heads calibrate under distribution shift?
Can editable generation exploit repository histories, proof revisions, or molecular-edit trajectories while respecting causal and physical validity?
What state representation lets a learned editor reuse memory without losing provenance needed to audit or reverse an incorrect deletion?

competitive_landscape.title: PENCIL: Long Thoughts with Short Memory
competitive_landscape.difference: PENCIL already adds a learned-token-triggered reduction rule to autoregressive reasoning, simulates Turing machines with O(T) generated tokens and O(S) maximum context, and empirically trains from solver traces on SAT, QBF, and Einstein puzzles. AP-MDM generalizes the memory-reuse idea to bidirectional parallel generation, arbitrary remask/insert/delete controls, and PRAM time-space analysis; its overwrite advantage over a strictly append-only ARM therefore should not be conflated with an advantage over PENCIL-style editable autoregression.

competitive_landscape.title: Levenshtein Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: LevT alternates parallel deletion, placeholder insertion, and token filling with a shared Transformer, trains the complementary policies by imitation learning, changes length dynamically, and unifies generation with refinement on translation, summarization, and post-editing. AP-MDM adds remasking, masked-diffusion framing, parallel-complexity theorems, and solver-trace tasks, but insert/delete sequence generation and learned loop termination were demonstrated six years earlier.

competitive_landscape.title: Remasking Discrete Diffusion Models with Inference-Time Scaling
competitive_landscape.difference: ReMDM derives a non-Markovian remasking posterior and plug-in schedules that reuse pretrained masked-diffusion weights, improving text, image, molecule, and LLaDA inference-time scaling without learning an edit head. AP-MDM learns remask controls and combines them with insertion/deletion plus formal memory-reuse claims, but supplies no comparable natural-language or large-model remasking evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Any-Order Flexible Length Masked Diffusion
competitive_landscape.difference: FlexMDM starts from the empty string, learns an insertion expectation and unmasking posterior through a joint stochastic interpolant, proves target-distribution and any-order sampling guarantees, and retrofits LLaDA-8B with gains on GSM8K and code infilling. AP-MDM offers the broader remask/insert/delete operation set and computational expressivity analysis; FlexMDM has stronger probabilistic grounding and real 8B evidence for variable length but does not address arbitrary memory rewrite or PSPACE simulation.

competitive_landscape.title: Edit Flows: Flow Matching with Edit Operations
competitive_landscape.difference: Edit Flows defines insertion, deletion, and substitution rates in a sequence-level CTMC, trains them tractably with auxiliary alignments and flow matching, and evaluates 280M-1.3B models on captions, text, and code. AP-MDM's mask-centric operations, learned backtracking, and PRAM analysis are distinct, but Edit Flows predates its all-edit framing and provides substantially stronger scaled generative evidence; AP-MDM instead excels on controlled algorithm-trace tasks.

competitive_landscape.title: Fine-Tuning Masked Diffusion for Provable Self-Correction
competitive_landscape.difference: PRISM learns a calibrated per-token quality scalar with a lightweight adapter and a provable likelihood target, then remasks low-quality tokens in the current state; current results cover Sudoku, 170M text, and 8B code. AP-MDM's remask bit is part of a more general edit controller and supports global formal simulations, but its proposed corruption-detection remask loss is not tested and has no explicit current-state quality guarantee. PRISM itself acknowledges that marginal token quality cannot capture global reasoning errors.

competitive_landscape.title: LLaDA2.1: Speeding Up Text Diffusion via Token Editing
competitive_landscape.difference: LLaDA2.1 trains a joint mask-to-token and token-to-token editor, revisits prior blocks, adds diffusion-specific RL, and demonstrates configurable speed-quality tradeoffs at 16B and 100B across 33 benchmarks. It lacks AP-MDM's variable-length insert/delete operations and complexity separations, but is decisive current evidence that direct rewriting scales far beyond AP-MDM's synthetic models and narrows any practical claim that learned token correction is unique to the proposed framework.

competitive_landscape.title: Learn from Your Mistakes: Self-Correcting Masked Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ProSeCo trains one MDM to correct samples from its own denoiser, interleaves full-token corrective loops with unmasking, and improves speed-quality tradeoffs on large math/code models, molecules, and unconditional text. AP-MDM covers insertion/deletion and stronger abstract computation claims, while ProSeCo supplies a much more realistic on-policy error distribution and extensive current evidence for learned rewriting; its main cost is a second training forward pass.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first systematic formal comparison of autoregressive, any-order masked-diffusion, and a provably more powerful any-process generation paradigm, with one mask-based framework that learns unmask, remask, insert, and delete operations without changing the Transformer backbone.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper's distinctive contribution is the unified resource analysis: an MDM-to-PRAM simulation, a controlled any-order-to-Masked-ARM serialization, a rewrite-enabled optimal-space PRAM simulation, an exact-support Dyck separation, and one operation interface exercised on backtracking, structural editing, and elimination traces. The formal coupling of parallel time, memory reuse, dynamic length, and generation process is broader than any one checked predecessor.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is strong in the combined complexity-theoretic framing and moderate in the model mechanism. PENCIL already establishes same-team erase-and-reuse theory for autoregression; LevT already learns insertion/deletion; ReMDM and PRISM learn or schedule remasking; FlexMDM provides principled masked insertion; Edit Flows already combines all major edit types at 1.3B scale. The component operations and motivation therefore are not new. What remains credibly new is their mask-centered unification with PRAM time-space analysis and the attempt to attribute benefits to parallelism, any-order choice, and rewrite separately. Practical superiority remains unproven because experiments use privileged synthetic traces, unmatched supervision, no uncertainty or compute accounting, and no scaled natural generation; subsequent LLaDA2.1 and ProSeCo provide stronger evidence that rewriting scales in real diffusion LMs. The exact-support and ARM-hardness claims also require narrow architectural assumptions, hardmax/two-mask modifications, and, for edit serialization, an unproved NC1-hardness conjecture.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass over all 56 extracted pages, including both OCR-recovered figure pages 49-50, every theorem statement and proof appendix, all four proposed self-supervised losses, the supervised trajectory construction, experiment tables, and task appendices. Source hashes match the locally indexed export.arxiv.org PDF; the official record was checked on 2026-08-23 as arXiv:2510.06190v2 (submitted 2025-11-17). Competitive search inspected current primary arXiv records and paper text for eight direct predecessors, concurrent systems, and 2026 successors; title snippets and secondary summaries were not used. Confidence is high in the operation definitions, asymptotic statements, and transcribed empirical numbers. Confidence in broad learnability and scaling claims is lower because the paper evaluates only synthetic solver traces and leaves the Sudoku transition-count and parity maximum-length inconsistencies unresolved. Author claims and reviewer inferences are labeled separately throughout.
